title: Education What We've Got Here Is Failure to Extrapolate Hill, Phil
author: Hill, Phil
summary: Phil Hill, an education technology analyst and architect of California's Online Education Initiative, critiques a CalMatters expose that documented genuine problems in California Community College online courses but committed a logical error in extrapolating those problems to the entire online modality. Hill argues that bad course design is a problem in any format, and the CalMatters framing -- treating isolated examples of poor online practice as representative of all 40% of online community college instruction -- risks a policy backlash that would harm students who depend on well-designed online courses. Drawing on research and interviews with former OEI/CVC executive directors, Hill identifies what a valid quality assessment of online education requires and argues it must distinguish modality from design quality. The real failure is not online education per se but the absence of institutional quality-control mechanisms that would catch bad courses before they become entrenched.
points: CalMatters documented genuine quality failures in specific community college online courses but made the analytical error of treating those failures as evidence against online education as a modality rather than as evidence of inadequate course design review processes.

Research on online learning effectiveness consistently shows modality effects are smaller than design and instructor quality effects -- a poorly designed in-person course will underperform a well-designed online course, and vice versa.

California's community college system lacks the institutional quality-control mechanisms -- peer course review, regular updating requirements, student feedback loops -- that would catch and correct bad online courses before they become entrenched.

The political risk of the CalMatters framing is a pendulum swing against online education that would harm working adults, students with caregiving responsibilities, and those in rural areas who depend on online courses for access.

Accurate quality assessment of online higher education requires disaggregating outcome data by course design, instructor professional development, and student support availability -- none of which a simple modality comparison captures.
quotes: **_Disclosure:_**_ While I have no business relationship with the California Community College system, I was involved in helping them set up the Online Education Initiative, which was renamed the California Virtual Campus. This post directly looks at the current state of online education in California, including information from the current and former executive directors of OEI / CVC based on _[_a podcast interview_](https://onedtech.philhillaa.com/podcast/s/the_on_edtech_plus_podcast/s01e05_...

So the real question is not "what's wrong with online education." It is how a course like this gets offered at all, inside a system that has spent more than a decade building an apparatus designed to avoid these problems. Since 2014, CCCS, through the Online Education Initiative that was renamed as the California Virtual Campus (CVC), have run a voluntary course-design rubric and a Peer Online Course Review process (POCR) that not only provides guidance on design but also puts faculty courses...

The failure CalMatters found is real -- but it is a failure of local commitment, a campus where the quality process is optional, and a department let an indefensible course run. It is not a failure of online education.

That study was based on the primary metric shared in CCC public data - course completion rates with grades of A, B, or C. This, of course, is not an ideal metric, which can be seen in the aforementioned microeconomics course example. Passing that course would be easy, whether you learned anything or not.

Furthermore, the pandemic presented an outlier, where most students were forced into online courses in "emergency remote learning" situations. **If you look at the pre- and post-pandemic years, what jumps out to me is the significant increase in performance for online course taking with much smaller increases for traditional, or face-to-face course taking. In fact, the performance gap has all but disappeared in the system.**

If the CalMatters' headline of "Community college students struggle with online education" refers to students having to work hard, then that would make sense. But what I believe they actually mean is that students are not succeeding because of online education.
